name: SCS (Splitting Conic Solver)
baseline: Clarabel 0.11.1 (interior point); the same page also times HiGHS 1.15.1, PIQP 0.6.4, OR-Tools PDLP 9.15, OSQP 1.1.3, ProxQP 0.7.3 and NVIDIA cuOpt 26.8.0. SuiteSparse (the guessed baseline) is not a baseline here: SCS vendors AMD and QDLDL from it.
workload: Wall-clock solve time to a verified 1e-4 accuracy on the 37 large LPs of Mittelmann's LP test set (100,000 to 126 million nonzeros, 1800 s limit, 4-core Modal container, or A100 80GB for the cuDSS backend), plus the largest quartile (40) of 157 Maros-Meszaros/QPLIB QPs; every returned solution re-checked against the problem data.
claimed_speedup: Mittelmann LP set, shifted geometric mean time (verified solves of 37): SCS GPU cuDSS 208 s (28), SCS CPU MKL Pardiso 431 s (24), PDLP 733 s (19), Clarabel 817 s (20), PIQP 1352 s (12), cuOpt 2086 s (7), HiGHS 2889 s (9); about 3.9x faster than Clarabel on GPU and 1.9x on CPU (derived from page data). Largest QP quartile at 1e-4: SCS GPU 9.4 s (38 solved), SCS CPU 12.8 s (38), Clarabel 12.6 s (37), PIQP 18.3 s (34), OSQP 29.4 s (32). Page text: 'SCS with cuDSS solves more instances than any other solver, in less than half the geometric mean time of the runner-up.'
hardware: CPU runs: identical 4-core Linux x86-64 Modal containers (CPU model not stated), scs wheel using MKL Pardiso; GPU runs: NVIDIA A100 80GB with 8 host cores; 64 GB memory containers on the Mittelmann set.
stars_or_usage: 638 stars; default CVXPY solver for SDP, exponential-cone and power-cone problems; PyPI and conda-forge packages
tradeoffs: First-order operator-splitting (ADMM with Anderson acceleration): moderate accuracy (1e-4 default) is cheap, tight tolerances are not. Interior-point codes are faster on small problems and at 1e-6, and are the better default for SDPs. The GPU result needs the NVIDIA cuDSS backend; spectral cones need a build flag.
caveats: First-party benchmark of SCS 3.3.1 on the author's own harness (bodono/solver_benchmarks, results in bodono/solver_benchmarks_results campaign scs33_2026-09, same author), published September 2026; CPU model and compiler flags are not stated (prebuilt PyPI wheels), so tier C and not A. SCS is not fastest overall: on all 349 LPs HiGHS has shifted geometric mean 5.0 s against 11.9 s for SCS CPU; on all 157 QPs Clarabel is 3.1 s and PIQP 3.7 s against 7.5 s for SCS CPU; on SDPs SCS is last in geometric mean (107.5 s against SDPA 38.2 s) though it solves the most (77 of 94). Each solver is shown from the run whose achieved accuracy is nearest the 1e-4 target (SCS at 1e-4, interior-point codes at 1e-6 or 1e-8); the page itself says the Mittelmann set was run with 1800 s limits on 4 cores, so simplex and interior-point codes time out far more than in Mittelmann's own multi-hour runs ('not a re-run of his benchmark'); failures are charged 3x the time limit in the geometric mean. SCS returned false certificates on QGROW7, QGROW22 and neos-4413714-turia (counted as failures). cuOpt's PDLP mostly fails the independent residual check (7 of 37 pass).

name: SHOGUN (k-means)
workload: k-means clustering time in seconds on the Madelon (4400 instances, 500 attributes) and Arcene datasets, from the scikit-learn project's ml-benchmarks suite; each benchmark run 10 times with extreme values removed (July 2011 results).
claimed_speedup: k-means: Madelon 0.68 s (Shogun) vs 1.34 s (scikit-learn), about 2.0x faster; Arcene 0.19 s vs 0.51 s, about 2.7x faster (ratios derived from page data). Shogun is not faster elsewhere in the same suite: SVM Madelon 5.63 s vs 5.20 s, Arcene 0.39 s vs 0.38 s; nearest neighbors Madelon 1.36 s vs 0.57 s, Arcene 0.22 s vs 0.09 s.
tradeoffs: Large C++ toolbox with SWIG-generated Python, Octave, Java and other interfaces; the library core is BSD-3-Clause with some optional GPL3 components (check which components a build pulls in).
caveats: Independent third-party suite (scikit-learn project's ml-benchmarks, code public in the benchmarks directory), but from July 2011 with Shogun 0.10.0 and scikit-learn 0.8 (both far out of date); compiler and flags are not stated, so B and not A. The result is run through the Python interfaces, so interface overhead is included. The page source has a comment 'Note: The shogun is failling ..' next to the k-means section and the Shogun inertia for Arcene is blank (Madelon inertia is 7.3x10^8 against 7.4x10^8 for scikit-learn), so the Arcene win is unconfirmed. One small-dataset pair only; the SVM and kNN rows show Shogun slower than scikit-learn. A milk documentation page (pythonhosted.org/milk/benchmarks.html, Core2 6600 2.40GHz, versions not stated, normalised times) shows the same direction for k-means (Shogun 2.02, scikits.learn 6.74).

name: Torch7
workload: LeNet CPU timing, per-batch gradient computation and forward pass at batch size 64, Torch with 12 threads against Caffe and Theano with 12 threads (Bahrampour et al., Robert Bosch research; the paper also covers AlexNet and a stacked autoencoder).
claimed_speedup: Paper conclusion: 'Torch results in best performance when comparing CPU times'. LeNet batch 64, ms gradient / forward, 12 threads: Torch 16.5 / 4.6 (arXiv v3; 31.6 / 14.0 in v1), Caffe 66.4 / 33.7, Theano 204.3 / 78.7; so about 4.0x faster than Caffe on gradient and 12x faster than Theano (derived from the v3 figures; about 2.1x and 6.5x on v1). Torch 1 thread: 46.1 / 18.1 (v3), 70.4 / 29.0 (v1). Neon 545.6 / 172.7 on one thread.
tradeoffs: Lua front end over C tensor libraries (TH, THNN); the README says 'Torch is not in active development' and that the C backend was rewritten as ATen inside PyTorch, so new work belongs there. Community described as 'close to non-existent' as of 2019.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: arxiv.org, openreview.net and ar5iv were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper was not opened; the numbers come from two WebSearch results (second one corroborated the Caffe, Theano and Neon rows and the v1 versus v3 Torch difference) and must be re-read on the paper. CPU model, library versions and build flags were not seen. Peer review is only an ICLR 2016 workshop track (v2) plus arXiv v3, 2015 vintage. In the reachable soumith/convnet-benchmarks README (6-core i7-5930K, Titan X) Torch-7 native GPU convolution is not faster than Caffe: AlexNet 342 ms vs 324 ms, Overfeat 878 vs 823, OxfordNet 1105 vs 1068, layer-wise 1265 vs 1231 ms; the fast rows there are cuDNN or fbfft kernels called through Torch bindings. The Theano paper (arXiv 1605.02688, via search snippet) reports Theano slightly faster than Torch on an LSTM benchmark.

name: volesti
baseline: VINCI 1.0.5 (exact polytope volume) and Cousins-Vempala's Matlab volume code (reference [12], Gaussian cooling, O*(n^3))
workload: Wall-clock time (mean of 100 runs) to approximate H-polytope volume with error about 1% (eps = 1) for cubes, cross polytopes, random polytopes, simplices and Birkhoff polytopes B8 to B15, against exact VINCI/birkhoff computation and against the Cousins-Vempala Matlab code (10 runs).
claimed_speedup: Abstract: 'Our publicly available code is significantly faster than exact computation and more accurate than existing approximation methods.' Table 1, VolEsti vs exact seconds: cross-10 1.58 vs 388.50 (about 250x), cross-11 5.19 vs 6141.40 (about 1180x), rv-8-12 0.59 vs 261.37, rv-10-13 1.24 vs 59.50, B8 192.97 vs 1920.00, cube-20 4.62 vs swap (exact ran out of memory); B9 exact 8 days vs 499.56 s; exact methods cannot handle d above 15. Table 7 vs Cousins-Vempala Matlab (seconds): cube-20 4.62 vs 21.48, cube-30 17.96 vs 49.24, cube-40 50.72 vs 88.09 (ratios derived from page data: 4.6x, 2.7x, 1.7x), with 4 to 100 times smaller error on cube-d for d above 70.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (C++ double arithmetic, Boost mt19937, GMP in the LP solver)
hardware: Intel Core i5-2400 3.1GHz, 6MB L2 cache, 8GB RAM, 64-bit Debian GNU/Linux
tradeoffs: Randomised approximation (hit-and-run random walks with iterative rounding and boundary oracles), not exact volume; relative error about 1% at eps = 1 and runtime grows steeply with dimension (cube-100 takes 1285 s). Source is LGPL-3.0, so linking is allowed but modifications to the library must be shared.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SoCG 2014, Emiris and Fisikopoulos 'Efficient random-walk methods for approximating polytope volume') but about the 2014 precursor code (then on sourceforge randgeom), not today's volesti; PDF read from the author's GitHub pages repo; compiler and flags missing so B and not A. Exact VINCI is faster on easy low-dimensional inputs (cube-10 0.01 s vs 0.42 s, simplices 0.01 to 0.02 s vs 0.56 to 907 s, rv-8-10 0.01 s vs 0.37 s). Approximate versus exact answers are not the same task. Against the Cousins-Vempala Matlab code VolEsti is slower at high dimension (cube-100 1285.08 s vs 884.43 s; B9 499.56 s vs 420.07 s; cube-60 and above slower) and does about 100 times more hit-and-run steps; that code was run with eps = 0.1 against eps = 1 for VolEsti. The repo README and docs carry no benchmark numbers.
